A.explanation: Line A falls by only about $10 \text{ kg m s}^{-1}$ in $2.0 \text{ s}$, giving a gradient magnitude of about $5 \text{ N}$, not $10 \text{ N}$.

B.explanation: Line B falls from $20 \text{ kg m s}^{-1}$ to zero in $2.0 \text{ s}$, so $\Delta p = 20 \text{ kg m s}^{-1}$ and $|dp/dt| = 10 \text{ N}$.

C.explanation: Line C falls from $10 \text{ kg m s}^{-1}$ to zero in $2.0 \text{ s}$, giving a gradient magnitude of only $5 \text{ N}$.

D.explanation: Line D falls from $5 \text{ kg m s}^{-1}$ to zero in $2.0 \text{ s}$, giving a gradient magnitude of only $2.5 \text{ N}$.

hints: Notice the axes are $p$ in $\text{kg m s}^{-1}$ against $t$ in $\text{s}$, so the gradient of each line is rate of change of momentum.
Recall that resultant force equals rate of change of momentum, $F = \Delta p / \Delta t$, so a $10 \text{ N}$ force for $2.0 \text{ s}$ must change momentum by $20 \text{ kg m s}^{-1}$.
Compare the total fall in $p$ from $t = 0$ to $t = 2.0 \text{ s}$ for lines A, B, C and D and check which fall equals $20 \text{ kg m s}^{-1}$.
walkthrough: The force is the gradient of a momentum-time graph because $F = dp/dt$. For a constant force the $p$-$t$ graph is a straight line with constant gradient.
The magnitude of the change in momentum must equal the impulse: $\Delta p = F \Delta t$.
Substitute $F = 10 \text{ N}$ and $\Delta t = 2.0 \text{ s}$: $\Delta p = 10 \times 2.0 = 20 \text{ kg m s}^{-1}$.
The momentum is decreasing, so the correct line must drop by $20 \text{ kg m s}^{-1}$ over $2.0 \text{ s}$, giving a gradient of $-10 \text{ kg m s}^{-2}$ or $-10 \text{ N}$.
Only the line starting at $20 \text{ kg m s}^{-1}$ at $t = 0$ and reaching zero at $t = 2.0 \text{ s}$ drops by $20 \text{ kg m s}^{-1}$. This is option B.
